Traumatic Injury of the CNS

Disease Index

🩸 Epidural Hemorrhage

LO 1–4 Arterial · MMA Age 20–30 peak Biconvex on CT
🎯 How Boards Would Word It
  • "Struck in the temple/side of the head... brief loss of consciousness... regains consciousness and seems fine... then rapidly deteriorates" → epidural hematoma until proven otherwise ("talk and die")
  • Lucid interval is the buzzword — but remember it's actually absent in over half of cases, so don't anchor on it being present
  • Ipsilateral blown pupil + contralateral hemiparesis = uncal (transtentorial) herniation compressing CN III and the cerebral peduncle
  • Rare trap answer: ipsilateral hemiparesis (same side as the blown pupil) = Kernohan notch, a false localizing sign
  • CT buzzwords: biconvex / lentiform / lens-shaped hyperdensity that does not cross suture lines
  • Vessel: almost always the middle meningeal artery, torn by a fracture near the pterion (thinnest part of the skull)
  • Young patient (20s–30s) is a deliberate age clue — dura isn't yet densely adherent to the calvarium
Natural History
Epidemiology & Etiology
  • Occurs in up to ~10% of moderate–severe traumatic brain injuries
  • Male : female ≈ 4:1
  • Peak age 20–30; uncommon after age 50 (dura becomes more densely adherent to the calvarium with age)
  • Traumatic (vast majority): MVC, falls, assault — usually a blow to the lateral/temporal skull
  • Nontraumatic (rare): coagulopathy, dural vascular malformation, infection, dural metastases
  • Source vessel: middle meningeal artery tear (branch of the maxillary artery) — by far the most common; usually at the pterion, the thinnest point of the skull. Venous EDH (middle meningeal vein, dural sinus) is rare and more often posterior fossa/vertex.
Pathophysiology
Blow to temporal skull
→
Skull fracture
→
MMA tear
→
Blood strips dura from calvarium (stopped at sutures)
Initial tamponade
→
Lucid interval
→
Continued expansion, ↑ICP
→
Uncal herniation
→
CN III + brainstem compression

Because the dura is tightly fixed at the cranial sutures, the hematoma is physically prevented from spreading past them — this is exactly why it stays biconvex/lens-shaped on imaging instead of spreading like a subdural bleed.

Pathophysiology — MMA tear beneath the pterion (left) strips the dura from the calvarium; the collection is confined by cranial sutures (right)
⚠ Prognosis if Untreated

Continued expansion → uncal herniation → brainstem compression → coma and death. Worse prognosis is associated with GCS ≤ 8 at presentation, pupillary abnormalities, longer time from herniation onset to decompression, age > 75, and larger hematoma volume with significant midline shift. Every hour of delay to decompression worsens outcome.

Clinical Presentation
Classic Course
  • Brief loss of consciousness at the moment of head injury
  • Lucid interval — return to normal/near-normal mentation — but present in only ~20–50% of patients (absent in the majority)
  • Rapid neurological decline: worsening headache, persistent vomiting, drowsiness, and altered mental status
  • Signs of rising ICP: Cushing triad (hypertension, bradycardia, irregular respirations)
  • Pupillary changes from uncal herniation: ipsilateral mydriasis (anisocoria) most common; can progress to bilateral fixed, dilated pupils
  • Contralateral hemiparesis (or, rarely, ipsilateral — Kernohan notch, a false localizing sign)
  • Signs of the associated skull fracture: scalp hematoma, CSF rhinorrhea/otorrhea, Battle sign, raccoon eyes
  • Untreated: coma → death
🚩 Red Flags

Rapid deterioration after a lucid interval ("talk and die") and any new pupillary asymmetry are neurosurgical emergencies — treat as impending herniation and escalate immediately rather than waiting on imaging in an unstable patient.

Diagnostic Workup
History / Physical ExamLabs / Imaging
Head trauma with a blow to the temporal/lateral skull; brief LOC ± lucid interval Noncontrast CT head — first-line: biconvex, sharply demarcated, hyperdense extra-axial lesion limited by suture lines, usually temporal/temporoparietal; look for an associated skull fracture
Anisocoria, contralateral (or rarely ipsilateral) motor deficit, Cushing triad CBC and coagulation panel — baseline, and essential if the patient is anticoagulated
Signs of basilar skull fracture (raccoon eyes, Battle sign, otorrhea/rhinorrhea) MRI head — if CT is equivocal or a small EDH is suspected with a normal initial CT; lesion is T2-hypointense
Suspected nontraumatic EDH Angiography — if a dural vascular malformation is suspected
CT head, noncontrast — biconvex hyperdense EDH (top: coronal; middle: axial), with the underlying parietal skull fracture visible on bone window (bottom)
CT head, axial — small acute EDH along the right frontal convexity
💡 Pearl

The initial CT can be falsely reassuring — a small arterial EDH (especially in the middle cranial fossa) or a venous EDH can be slow to accumulate. Any clinical deterioration after a normal initial scan warrants an immediate repeat CT.

Treatment
Management Overview

EDH is a neurosurgical emergency — hematoma expansion can rapidly progress to herniation and death. Neuroprotective stabilization takes priority over diagnostic workup, and all patients require emergency neurosurgical consultation.

Medical / Neuroprotective

  • ABCDE trauma survey, cervical spine precautions
  • Neuroprotective measures: head-of-bed elevation, maintain normotension/normoxia/normocapnia
  • Stop antithrombotic agents; reverse anticoagulation
  • Tranexamic acid if GCS 9–13 and < 3 hours since injury

Surgical

  • Definitive: urgent craniotomy, hematoma evacuation, and ligation of the bleeding vessel
  • Temporizing: skull trephination (burr hole) if no neurosurgeon on site and signs of herniation/GCS ≤ 8, followed by urgent transfer
  • Indications: volume > 30 mL, thickness > 15 mm, midline shift > 5 mm, GCS ≤ 8, focal deficit, or evidence of herniation

Pharmaceutical

  • Mannitol or hypertonic saline for elevated ICP
  • Tranexamic acid (see above criteria)
  • Preoperative antibiotic prophylaxis (e.g., cefazolin) before craniotomy

Conservative Management

  • Reserved for small, asymptomatic EDH with GCS > 8 and none of the surgical criteria above
  • Admit to neuro-ICU/ICU; frequent GCS checks for ≥ 72 hours
  • Serial CT: repeat in 4–6 hours if stable, immediately if any deterioration
  • Escalate to craniotomy if the hematoma progresses on observation
Serial CT — a small EDH on the initial scan (top) expands significantly on follow-up (bottom), with new mass effect — the rationale for close interval re-imaging during conservative management
OMM Note

Osteopathic manipulative techniques — particularly cranial approaches and any technique capable of altering intracranial pressure — are contraindicated in the acute setting of a suspected or confirmed intracranial hemorrhage.

🧠 Practice Questions — Epidural Hemorrhage

🩸 Acute Subdural Hemorrhage

LO 1–4 Venous · Bridging Veins Onset ≤ 3 days Crescent on CT
🎯 How Boards Would Word It
  • Elderly patient on anticoagulation after a minor fall, or a young patient after a high-speed MVC/rapid deceleration — note that "the head didn't even have to strike anything" for shear forces to tear a bridging vein
  • Don't lean on a lucid interval here — it's present in only ~12–40% of acute SDH, far less reliable a clue than in EDH
  • Alcohol use disorder or dementia in an elderly patient = cerebral atrophy stretching the bridging veins, making them more prone to tearing even with trivial trauma
  • CT buzzwords: crescent-shaped / concave hyperdensity that CAN cross suture lines but does NOT cross the midline — the exact mirror image of EDH
  • Vessel: bridging veins (venous, not arterial) draining the cortex into the dural sinuses
  • Boards love this exact pairing: "acute SDH and acute EDH can look clinically identical — the CT is what tells them apart."
Natural History
Epidemiology & Etiology
  • Traumatic acute SDH occurs in ~20–30% of patients with severe traumatic brain injury; incidence roughly 3 per 10,000 in the US
  • Male : female ≈ 3:1
  • Seen across a wide age range — more common in younger adults (30–50, high-energy trauma) but also common in the elderly (falls, cerebral atrophy) and in infants (birth trauma, shaken baby syndrome)
  • Most common cause: blunt head trauma (e.g., MVC) causing rupture of the bridging veins
  • Acceleration–deceleration injury alone can tear bridging veins — the head does not need to strike an object
  • Nonaccidental trauma (shaken baby syndrome) is an important cause in infants
  • Risk factors: anticoagulant/antiplatelet therapy or coagulopathy, advanced age, cerebral atrophy, alcohol use disorder
Pathophysiology
Head trauma / rapid deceleration
→
Shear force stretches & tears bridging veins
→
Low-pressure venous bleeding into subdural space
→
Crescent-shaped collection, crosses sutures, stops at midline (falx)

The subdural space (between dura and arachnoid) isn't anchored at the cranial sutures the way the epidural space is, so blood spreads freely across suture lines — but it is stopped at the midline by the dural reflection of the falx cerebri. This is the exact opposite imaging pattern from an epidural hematoma.

Etiology — a torn bridging vein (left, circled) bleeds into the subdural space, producing a hematoma that spreads along the convexity beneath the dura (right)
⚠ Prognosis if Untreated

Can progress rapidly to cerebral herniation, coma, and death. Acute SDH carries a higher likelihood of underlying parenchymal brain injury than acute EDH, and as a result generally has a worse prognosis.

Clinical Presentation
Classic Course
  • By definition, symptom onset within 3 days of the inciting event
  • Lucid interval in only ~12–40% of patients — much less reliable than in EDH
  • Impaired consciousness and confusion, which can rapidly progress to coma
  • Focal neurological signs: contralateral hemiparesis with UMN signs (rarely ipsilateral — Kernohan syndrome, the same false-localizing phenomenon seen in EDH)
  • Cranial nerve findings: diplopia, blurred vision, anisocoria, anosmia
  • Slurred or disorganized speech
  • Signs of rising ICP: headache, vomiting, Cushing triad
  • Cerebral herniation signs: abnormal posturing (decorticate/decerebrate), seizures
🚩 Red Flags

Traumatic acute SDH and acute EDH can be clinically indistinguishable — neuroimaging is what differentiates them. Any rapid decline, new pupillary asymmetry, or posturing is a neurosurgical emergency.

Diagnostic Workup
History / Physical ExamLabs / Imaging
High-energy trauma or rapid deceleration (impact not required); elderly patient on anticoagulation after a minor fall; concerning trauma history in an infant Noncontrast CT head — first-line: crescent-shaped, concave, sharply demarcated extra-axial lesion; can cross suture lines, does not cross the midline
Altered consciousness, focal deficits, pupillary changes, posturing Density reflects the age of the bleed: acute = hyperdense, subacute = isodense, chronic = hypodense, acute-on-chronic = mixed density
Screen for other injuries (skull fracture, concurrent EDH, cerebral edema) CBC, coagulation panel, electrolytes — baseline and essential if anticoagulated
Neuro findings unexplained by CT, suspected subacute/chronic component MRI head — T2 signal also tracks blood age (acute hypointense, subacute hyperintense, chronic hyperintense core with hypointense rim)
CT head, axial — classic crescent-shaped hyperdense acute SDH along the right convexity
CT head, axial — larger acute SDH with midline shift and a small amount of intraventricular blood, reflecting greater mass effect
Acute-on-chronic SDH — hyperdense (recent bleed) and hypodense (older, degraded clot) components admixed within the same collection, illustrating how CT density tracks the age of the blood
💡 Pearl — EDH vs. SDH on Imaging

EDH: biconvex/lentiform, does not cross suture lines. SDH: crescent/concave, can cross suture lines but does not cross the midline. Same trauma, opposite shapes — this comparison is a favorite board question.

Treatment
Management Overview

Symptomatic SDH at any stage warrants immediate neurosurgical consultation; asymptomatic SDH still needs an urgent consult to decide between surgical and conservative management.

Medical / Neuroprotective

  • ABCDE survey, cervical spine precautions until cleared
  • Neuroprotective measures and empiric ICP management if signs of ↑ICP
  • Stop antithrombotics; reverse anticoagulation; consider platelet transfusion if platelets < 100,000/mm³
  • Tranexamic acid if GCS 9–13 and < 3 hours since injury

Surgical

  • Indications: hematoma ≥ 10 mm, midline shift ≥ 5 mm, herniation signs, GCS drop ≥ 2 points, fixed dilated pupil(s), ICP > 20 mmHg, or failed conservative management
  • Ideally within ≤ 4 hours of the inciting event
  • Craniotomy with hematoma evacuation ± decompressive craniectomy
  • Temporizing burr hole craniotomy if transfer to definitive care is required and herniation signs are present
Large subdural collection with significant mass effect and effacement of the underlying gyri — the size and mass effect here meet criteria for surgical evacuation even without waiting for further decline

Pharmaceutical

  • Tranexamic acid (see criteria above)
  • Anticoagulant reversal agents specific to the agent involved
  • Mannitol or hypertonic saline for elevated ICP

Conservative Management

  • Asymptomatic, hematoma < 10 mm, midline shift < 5 mm, normal pupils, no signs of ↑ICP
  • Admit to neurocritical care; ICP monitoring; serial neuro exams
  • Repeat neuroimaging within 36 hours, or sooner with any deterioration
OMM Note

As with epidural hematoma, osteopathic manipulative techniques — especially cranial approaches or anything that could alter intracranial pressure — are contraindicated in the acute setting of a suspected or confirmed intracranial hemorrhage.

🧠 Practice Questions — Acute Subdural Hemorrhage

🩸 Chronic Subdural Hemorrhage

LO 1–4 Onset ≥ 21 days Elderly · > 60 Hypodense on CT
🎯 How Boards Would Word It
  • Elderly patient (or chronic alcoholic) brought in by family for weeks of progressive confusion, personality change, and gait instability/recurrent falls — this is the classic "looks like new-onset dementia" trap
  • A history of a minor fall or head bump weeks earlier that the patient or family barely remembers or never mentioned is the buried clue
  • Anticoagulation in an elderly patient is the classic risk-factor pairing
  • CT buzzwords: crescent-shaped, HYPODENSE extra-axial collection that crosses suture lines — hypodense is the key word distinguishing it from acute SDH's hyperdensity
  • The vignette is designed to make you chase a dementia or stroke workup — the CT is what reveals the true culprit
  • Treatment buzzword: burr-hole drainage is often curative, since the clot has liquefied and organized over weeks (unlike the solid clot of acute SDH)
Natural History
Epidemiology & Etiology
  • Estimated incidence ~1 per 10,000 individuals; more broadly cited at 2–13 per 100,000 population
  • ~95% of cases occur in patients over age 60; most common in individuals older than 70
  • Male : female ≈ 2:1
  • Can follow only minor head trauma — often trivial enough that it isn't recalled or reported
  • Risk factors: anticoagulant/antiplatelet therapy or coagulopathy, chronic alcohol use disorder, advanced age, cerebral atrophy, epilepsy, hyponatremia, neurodegenerative disease, prior TBI
  • In infants: nonaccidental trauma (shaken baby syndrome), birth trauma, meningitis
  • Individuals at the extremes of age (infants and the elderly) carry the highest risk of nontraumatic chronic SDH
Pathophysiology
Minor (often unrecalled) head trauma
→
Slow bleeding from stretched, atrophy-vulnerable bridging veins
→
Hematoma organizes over days–weeks; fragile outer/inner neomembranes form
→
Repeated microhemorrhages from these fragile vessels + osmotic fluid shifts
→
Gradual enlargement, insidious mass effect

Cerebral atrophy (age, alcohol use disorder, neurodegenerative disease) widens the subdural space, giving the brain more room to shift and stretching the bridging veins — which is why even trivial trauma can tear them in this population.

Anatomy — the subdural hematoma sits between the dura mater and the arachnoid space, along the brain's convexity
Conceptual illustration — a subdural collection compressing the adjacent cortex (shown here as fresh red blood for clarity; a true chronic SDH is older, degraded blood that appears hypodense rather than this hyperdense red on actual imaging)
⚠ Prognosis if Untreated

Prognosis is generally better than acute SDH, but chronic SDH still carries increasing mortality with advancing age, and a large or bilateral collection can progress to coma. Recurrence after drainage is common, especially in elderly or anticoagulated patients.

Clinical Presentation
Classic Course
  • Insidious onset — by definition, symptoms begin ≥ 3 weeks after the inciting event, which is often a minor trauma the patient doesn't recall or report
  • Altered mental status: confusion, delirium, excessive drowsiness, progressing to coma if severe
  • Recurrent headaches
  • Cognitive deficits: impaired memory, a dementia-like picture
  • Focal neurological signs: contralateral hemiparesis (most common), which can progress to hemiplegia; dysphasia
  • Incontinence, ataxia, and recurrent falls — which can also become part of a vicious cycle of re-injury
  • Personality changes
  • Seizures (rare)
  • Unilateral pupillary dilation with oculomotor paresis, bradycardia, and hypertension can occur with larger collections or significant mass effect
🚩 Red Flags

Chronic SDH is a classic mimicker of dementia, depression, or stroke in older adults. Always consider it in an elderly or anticoagulated patient with subacute cognitive decline, personality change, gait instability, or new falls — even without a clearly recalled head injury.

Diagnostic Workup
History / Physical ExamLabs / Imaging
Elderly patient, alcohol use disorder, or anticoagulation with subacute cognitive/personality change, recent falls, or a history (even unclear) of minor head trauma Noncontrast CT head — first-line: crescent-shaped, hypodense, sharply demarcated extra-axial lesion that crosses suture lines; assess for mass effect (ventricular compression, midline shift)
Focal deficits (hemiparesis, dysphasia), incontinence, ataxia CBC, coagulation panel, electrolytes — baseline, and to evaluate for chronic blood loss or coagulopathy
Suspected mixed-age bleed (new symptoms on a background of chronic decline) Acute-on-chronic pattern possible: hyperdense (recent) areas admixed with hypodense (older) areas
Diagnosis unclear on CT, or need to exclude a CSF collection MRI — T2 hyperintense core with a hypointense rim in chronic SDH; helps distinguish it from a subdural hygroma
CT head, axial, brain window — large crescent-shaped, hypodense chronic SDH over the lateral hemisphere, crossing cranial sutures, with compression of the adjacent lateral ventricle
💡 Pearl — Chronic SDH vs. Subdural Hygroma

A subdural hygroma (a CSF collection from an arachnoid tear after head injury) can look very similar to a chronic SDH on CT and is a key differential to keep in mind — symptomatic hygromas are also managed with surgical drainage. Also keep other causes of subacute cognitive decline (neurodegenerative disease, ischemic stroke) on the differential until imaging clarifies the picture.

Treatment
Management Overview

An unconscious or acutely decompensating patient is a medical emergency requiring immediate ABC stabilization. Otherwise, management centers on the same size/mass-effect criteria used in acute SDH, with drainage of the (now liquefied) collection as the mainstay of definitive treatment.

Medical

  • ABC stabilization if the patient is obtunded or unconscious — treat as a medical emergency
  • Correct reversible risk factors: stop/reverse anticoagulation, correct coagulopathy
  • Address underlying contributors (blood pressure control, glycemic control, alcohol use)

Surgical

  • Indications: hematoma ≥ 10 mm or midline shift ≥ 5 mm (operate even if asymptomatic), or symptomatic with mass effect, increasing size, or a change from baseline neurological status
  • Burr hole drainage / twist drill craniostomy — first-line, since the organized, liquefied clot drains well through a small opening; especially favored in elderly or high-surgical-risk patients
  • Craniotomy with clot evacuation (± drain) for more solid or recurrent collections

Pharmaceutical

  • Mannitol if acutely elevated ICP
  • Dexamethasone (corticosteroids) — may aid spontaneous regression of the hematoma, particularly useful as an adjunct or in poor surgical candidates

Conservative Management

  • Small, asymptomatic collections (< 10 mm, midline shift < 5 mm, normal pupils, no signs of ↑ICP)
  • Close monitoring with serial imaging
  • Address reversible risk factors; corticosteroids may be trialed
  • Escalate to surgery if the patient becomes symptomatic
OMM Note

As with acute intracranial hemorrhage, osteopathic manipulative techniques — particularly cranial approaches or anything capable of altering intracranial pressure — should be avoided in a patient with a known or suspected chronic subdural hematoma until cleared by neurosurgery.

🧠 Practice Questions — Chronic Subdural Hemorrhage

🧠 Traumatic Brain Injury

LO 1–6 GCS-Based Severity Primary vs. Secondary Injury Falls = #1 cause
🎯 How Boards Would Word It
  • GCS cutoffs are vocabulary, not trivia — mild 13–15, moderate 9–12, severe ≤ 8. Expect a stem giving you E/V/M components to add up yourself.
  • Raccoon eyes (anterior fossa) vs. Battle sign + hemotympanum (posterior fossa/temporal bone) — vignettes love a physical exam photo here
  • CSF rhinorrhea/otorrhea with a "halo sign" (a clear ring around a blood spot on gauze or a pillowcase) = dural tear
  • Decorticate ("CORe flexion," lesion above the red nucleus, better prognosis) vs. decerebrate (lesion at/below the red nucleus in the pons, worse prognosis) — a classic paired question
  • Diffuse axonal injury: high-speed rotational/deceleration trauma → comatose patient with a deceptively normal initial CT — MRI is the answer they're fishing for
  • Coup-contrecoup: injury at the site of impact AND on the opposite side, from the brain rebounding inside the skull
  • Cushing triad (hypertension, bradycardia, irregular respirations) = impending herniation, a late and ominous finding
Natural History
Epidemiology & Etiology
  • Incidence of TBI ≈ 800 per 100,000; roughly 10 million head injuries occur annually in the US, about 20% severe enough to cause brain injury
  • Trauma is the leading cause of death in individuals under 45, and over half of these deaths involve head trauma
  • Most common in young children (0–4 years), teenagers/young adults (15–24), and adults over 65 (course notes emphasize the very young < 5 and very old > 85 as peak groups)
  • Male > female
  • A skull fracture increases the likelihood of underlying brain injury 5- to 10-fold
  • Falls — the leading overall cause, especially in children and the elderly
  • Motor vehicle accidents — second most common cause overall, but the most common cause of the most severe injuries
  • Contact sports; interpersonal violence
  • Penetrating injury: high-velocity (gunshot) or low-velocity (assault, foreign body)
  • Blast injury (high-pressure wave from an explosion) — seen in military/war-zone settings
Pathophysiology — Primary vs. Secondary Injury

Primary brain injury — occurs immediately at the moment of trauma:

  • Focal: intracranial hemorrhage (EDH, SDH, SAH, ICH), cerebral contusion (coup-contrecoup), parenchymal lacerations
  • Diffuse: mild TBI/concussion, cerebral edema, diffuse axonal injury (DAI) — multifocal shearing/tearing of axons from rotational acceleration-deceleration forces, classically at the gray-white junction, corpus callosum, and brainstem; can look deceptively normal on initial CT and often requires MRI to identify

Secondary brain injury — indirect, physiological, and partially preventable:

  • Disrupted blood-brain barrier, hypoxic-ischemic injury, cerebral edema, rising ICP, ischemia, inflammation, infection
Trauma
→
Primary injury (focal or diffuse)
→
Secondary cascade (edema, BBB disruption, ischemia, ↑ICP)
→
Herniation if unchecked

Neuroprotective measures throughout TBI management exist specifically to interrupt this secondary cascade — it's the one part of the injury we can still influence after the initial trauma has already happened.

⚠ Prognosis
  • Mild TBI: 80–90% of patients make a full recovery within 2 weeks
  • Moderate TBI: 90% improve, but ~44% are left with moderate disability; 10% deteriorate to severe TBI
  • Severe TBI: mortality ≈ 35%
Clinical Presentation
General Symptoms
  • Loss of consciousness or altered consciousness (confusion, disorientation), possibly with a lucid interval
  • Headache, amnesia
  • Signs of ↑ICP, altered mood/behavior (e.g., aggression), dizziness, nausea, vomiting
  • Cushing triad and cerebral herniation syndromes
  • Focal deficits depending on the affected region: contralateral hemiparesis/hemiplegia, contralateral sensory loss, cranial nerve palsies (diplopia, blurred vision, anisocoria, anosmia), dysarthria, impaired coordination
Abnormal PosturingDecorticate (Flexor)Decerebrate (Extensor)
DescriptionBilateral upper extremity flexion, lower extremity extensionBilateral upper and lower extremity extension
Lesion siteProximal brainstem, above the red nucleusDistal brainstem/pons, at or below the red nucleus
Overactive tractRubrospinal + vestibulospinalVestibulospinal only
PrognosisBetterWorse
Decorticate vs. decerebrate posturing — a lesion above the red nucleus spares rubrospinal-driven flexion (decorticate); a lesion at or below it leaves only extension (decerebrate). Mnemonic: deCORticate = arms flex toward the CORe.
Signs of Associated Injury
  • Skull fracture: scalp hematoma/laceration, liquorrhea (CSF leak through a dural tear — may show a "halo sign" on gauze)
  • Anterior basilar skull fracture: CSF rhinorrhea, raccoon eyes, palsies of CN I, V, VI, VII, and/or VIII
  • Posterior basilar skull fracture: CSF otorrhea, hemotympanum, Battle sign, palsies of CN VI, VII, and/or VIII
  • Facial fractures: hematoma, swelling, epistaxis, visible deformity
Bilateral periorbital ecchymosis ("raccoon eyes") — a sign of anterior basilar skull fracture
Longitudinal (blue) vs. transverse (red) temporal bone fracture patterns through the petrous bone — the fracture line's relationship to the labyrinth/facial nerve canal predicts which cranial nerves are at risk
Hemotympanum — blood behind an intact tympanic membrane, a sign of posterior basilar skull fracture
🚩 Red Flags

GCS ≤ 12, focal neurologic deficits, deteriorating status, abnormal posturing, altered mood/behavior, dizziness/nausea/vomiting, Cushing triad, cerebral herniation, SBP < 90 mmHg, CSF rhinorrhea/otorrhea, Battle sign/raccoon eyes, hemotympanum, and seizures all warrant urgent evaluation and escalation.

Diagnostic Workup
History / Physical ExamLabs / Imaging
Mechanism, GCS, pupillary exam, lateralizing signs, SAMPLE history, duration of amnesia, anticoagulant use Noncontrast CT head — first-line. Always indicated for GCS ≤ 12; for GCS ≥ 13, only if mTBI imaging criteria are met, or with an open injury, depressed fracture, or rapid neurological deterioration
CT brain window findings Hemorrhage/hematoma (hyperdense), mass effect (parenchymal compression, midline shift), herniation, DAI (punctate hyperdensities at the gray-white junction, corpus callosum, brainstem — can be normal early), contusion (heterogeneous lesion with surrounding edema), diffuse cerebral edema (ventricular compression, effaced sulci/gyri, effaced basal cisterns)
CT bone window findings Skull fractures (linear, depressed, or basilar), pneumocephalus
Symptoms unexplained by CT, or subacute/chronic deficits MRI head — preferred for microhemorrhage, DAI, and contusions
Suspected C-spine injury, CSF leak, or vascular injury CT C-spine; CT maxillofacial/temporal bone; CT or MR angiography (blunt cerebrovascular injury, CTA "spot sign" for active hemorrhage)
Altered consciousness; suspected coagulopathy or major blood loss Point-of-care glucose, blood alcohol level, urine toxicology, BMP, ABG, coagulation panel, type & screen; pregnancy test in women of childbearing age
Subdural hematoma with cerebral edema — hyperdense crescent-shaped SDH with an accompanying scalp hematoma, extensive hypodense cerebral edema, sulcal effacement, and midline shift with compressed anterior/dilated posterior ventricular horns
Bilateral, asymmetric hypodensity consistent with cerebral contusion/edema — a reminder that coup-contrecoup injury can produce findings on both sides of the brain from a single impact
💡 Pearl — The Normal CT Trap

A comatose patient with a normal initial head CT should raise suspicion for diffuse axonal injury, not reassure you that nothing is wrong — DAI is a diffuse, microscopic process that CT is poorly suited to detect. MRI (or diffusion tensor imaging) is far more sensitive.

Treatment
Management Overview

The primary survey (ABCDE) runs simultaneously with neuroprotective measures, which take precedence over diagnostics. Definitive management then depends on TBI severity and CT findings.

Medical / Neuroprotective

  • C-spine immobilization as needed
  • Maintain SpO2 > 92–94%, PaO2 > 60 mmHg, PaCO2 35–45 mmHg
  • Maintain SBP 90–180 mmHg — avoid hypotension; permissive hypotension is harmful in TBI
  • Maintain glucose 80–180 mg/dL
  • Consider intubation if GCS ≤ 8 (ketamine preferred as an induction agent if no signs of ↑ICP)
  • Avoid hypothermia

Surgical

  • Craniotomy and evacuation for EDH/SDH meeting surgical criteria — done as soon as possible
  • Decompressive craniectomy for intraparenchymal or posterior fossa hemorrhage with mass effect, neurological deterioration, or ICP refractory to medical therapy
  • Extraventricular drain (EVD) for ICP management
  • Depressed skull fracture surgery if: open with dural penetration, significant depression, significant cranial hematoma, frontal sinus involvement, gross contamination/infection, pneumocephalus, or major cosmetic deformity

Pharmaceutical

  • Tranexamic acid if GCS 9–13 and < 3 hours since injury (unlikely to benefit severe TBI)
  • Anticoagulant/antiplatelet reversal — target INR ≤ 1.4; contraindicated with concomitant cerebral venous thrombosis
  • Seizure prophylaxis (phenytoin or levetiracetam) for 7 days in severe TBI
  • Analgesics, antiemetics, sedation as needed

Disposition

  • Mild: ED observation; admit if GCS < 15 at 2 hours or other admission criteria met
  • Moderate/Severe: admit/transfer to neurocritical care; follow-up imaging at 12–24h (moderate, or sooner if deterioration/abnormal initial scan/↑ICP/coagulopathy/hypotension) or 6h (severe)
OMM Note

As with any acute intracranial pathology, osteopathic manipulative techniques that could alter intracranial pressure are contraindicated until the patient has been cleared by neurosurgery.

Monitoring & Long-Term Complications
Monitoring
  • Continuous or frequent vitals monitoring; frequent reassessment of GCS, glucose, and electrolytes
  • Invasive ICP monitoring if GCS ≤ 8 with signs of ↑ICP on CT, or a normal CT plus ≥ 2 of: age > 40, unilateral/bilateral motor posturing, SBP < 90 mmHg
  • Standardized pain and sedation scales (e.g., RASS)
  • DVT prophylaxis: mechanical if there's an active intracranial bleed; pharmacologic (LMWH or low-dose unfractionated heparin) after individualized risk-benefit assessment once stable
Complications
  • Cerebral edema, coma, permanent focal neurological deficits (including persistent vegetative state)
  • Post-concussion syndrome
  • Early post-traumatic seizures (within 1 week) and late post-traumatic seizures (after 1 week)
  • Acute traumatic coagulopathy
  • Chronic CSF rhinorrhea
  • Intracranial infection (meningitis, encephalitis, brain abscess) and surgical site infection
  • Irreversible loss of brain function (brain death)
Paroxysmal Sympathetic Hyperactivity (PSH)

Loss of cortical inhibition of the sympathetic nervous system after acute brain injury (most commonly TBI) produces recurrent, self-limited episodes (typically starting about a week post-injury, lasting up to 30 minutes) of fever, tachycardia, tachypnea, hypertension, and muscle spasms/posturing. Treatment is supportive (antipyretics, hydration, reducing triggering stimuli) plus opioids, sympatholytics (clonidine, propranolol), benzodiazepines, or muscle relaxants (dantrolene, baclofen) depending on symptoms.

Prevention & Health Promotion
Risk Reduction
  • Seatbelt use and avoidance of drunk driving
  • Helmet use for motorcyclists, cyclists, and contact-sport athletes
  • Fall-prevention strategies in the elderly (home safety modification, vision correction, medication review)
  • Reduction of interpersonal violence
  • Return-to-play protocols after concussion to avoid repeat injury before recovery
🧠 Practice Questions — Traumatic Brain Injury

🦴 Traumatic Spinal Cord Injury

LO 1–6 M:F ≈ 4:1 Avg. Age ~31–41y Cervical Most Vulnerable

Injury to the spinal cord from external trauma to the vertebral canal or an internally expanding mass lesion. Rarely life-threatening in itself, but potentially devastating — rendering a patient paraplegic or quadriplegic — with recovery closely tied to how quickly the cord is decompressed. This topic covers compressive lesions; non-compressive (vascular or inflammatory) cord disease is covered separately.

🎯 How Boards Would Word It
  • Elderly patient with cervical spondylosis who falls and hyperextends the neck, presenting with upper extremity weakness much worse than lower extremity weakness = central cord syndrome, the most common incomplete pattern
  • Penetrating trauma causing hemisection → ipsilateral motor + proprioceptive loss with contralateral pain/temperature loss — the "crossed" findings are the giveaway for Brown-Séquard
  • Anterior spinal artery territory injury → motor + pain/temperature loss with the dorsal columns spared (proprioception and light touch still intact) — a classic "what's preserved" trap
  • Conus medullaris vs. cauda equina: both cause bowel/bladder/sexual dysfunction, but conus gives only mild, often symmetric lower-extremity motor loss with saddle anesthesia, while cauda equina gives a pure lower motor neuron pattern — flaccid, areflexic, and often asymmetric
  • Sacral sparing (voluntary anal contraction, intact deep anal pressure) on rectal exam means the injury is not a complete (AIS A) lesion, regardless of how little else works
  • "Time is cord": decompression within 24 hours more than doubles the odds of meaningful neurologic improvement
  • Autonomic dysreflexia (injuries above T6, triggered by a distended bladder or bowel) is a classic paired vignette — sudden severe hypertension and bradycardia with flushing above the lesion
Natural History
Epidemiology
  • Incidence ~28–55 per million population (up to ~40–54 in more recent estimates); roughly 10,000–17,730 new US cases per year
  • Prevalence estimated at 183,000–300,000 individuals
  • Average age at injury ~31–41 years; male : female ≈ 4:1; the affected population is trending older over time
Etiology

Acute Compressive

  • Motor vehicle accidents — leading cause (~36–48%)
  • Falls (~17–27%, increasingly common in the elderly)
  • Violence (~5–29%)
  • Recreational/sports activities (~7–16%)

Other Acute/Subacute

  • Iatrogenic (surgical injury)
  • Spinal epidural abscess
  • Spinal epidural hematoma
  • Spinal epidural neoplasm

Chronic Compressive

  • Spondylotic myelopathy — one of the most common causes of progressive cord compression
  • Syringomyelia

Anatomic Notes

  • ~20% of spinal column injuries affect more than one level
  • Cervical spine most vulnerable (greater mobility, less structural support) — ~⅔ of tSCI involve the cervical cord
Pathophysiology — A Two-Phase Injury

Primary injury: direct mechanical/compressive forces (contusion, compression, laceration, distraction) disrupt neural tissue — immediate neuronal/axonal damage, demyelination, and disruption of the blood-spinal cord barrier.

Secondary injury: unfolds over hours to weeks and is the target of most acute interventions.

Hypoperfusion/ischemia spreading from the lesion
→
Glutamate excitotoxicity + ionic imbalance
→
Oxidative stress, free radicals, lipid peroxidation
Inflammatory infiltration (microglia, astrocytes, neutrophils, T cells)
→
Apoptotic cascades — progressive cell death
→
Cystic cavitation + glial scar (blocks regeneration)
Classification Framework

By Location

  • Intramedullary — within the cord itself
  • Extramedullary — within the canal but outside the cord

By Level

  • Cervical, thoracic, lumbar, sacral cord, or conus medullaris — each with a distinct presentation (see Clinical Presentation)

By Pattern

  • Complete transection vs. a set of named incomplete syndromes (see Clinical Presentation)
⚠ Prognosis — Set Largely by Initial Severity
Initial AIS Grade1-Year Improvement Rate
A (complete)~19% — most show no improvement in neurologic grade and minimal motor recovery
B~74%
C~87%
D~47%

Most neurological recovery occurs within the first 6–9 months, fastest in the first 3 months. Thoracic-level and penetrating injuries carry a poorer prognosis. Historically, before modern management, mortality was extremely high — largely from respiratory and urological complications.

Clinical Presentation
General Features
  • Sensory loss, numbness, and paresthesias in a dermatomal "level-down" pattern from the point of injury
  • Motor loss — paresis/paralysis with segmental-level flaccidity and spasticity below the lesion (an upper motor neuron pattern)
  • Gait imbalance; bladder and bowel dysfunction; altered sexual function; chronic pain syndromes
  • Respiratory compromise, especially with high cervical lesions
Level of InjuryClinical Result
Above C4Quadriplegia with respiratory failure (diaphragm paralysis)
C4 to upper thoracicQuadriplegia, variable upper-extremity involvement
Thoracic region / conus medullarisParaplegia involving the lower extremities
Incomplete Spinal Cord Syndromes

Central Cord (~14%)

  • Most common incomplete syndrome
  • Upper extremity weakness > lower extremity weakness
  • Classic setup: elderly patient, cervical spondylosis, hyperextension injury

Brown-Séquard (~2%)

  • Hemisection: ipsilateral motor + proprioceptive loss, contralateral pain/temperature loss
  • Best prognosis among the incomplete syndromes

Anterior Cord (~6.5%)

  • Anterior spinal artery territory
  • Motor + pain/temperature loss with dorsal column sparing (proprioception, light touch preserved)

Conus Medullaris

  • Bladder/bowel/sexual dysfunction
  • Perineal (saddle) sensory loss
  • Only mild lower-extremity motor symptoms

Cauda Equina

  • Lower motor neuron pattern — flaccid paralysis, areflexic bowel/bladder
  • Variable, often asymmetric lower-extremity sensory loss
Diagnostic Workup
Imaging

CT is the preferred initial study — fracture, subluxation, bony damage. MRI is complementary — ligamentous injury, disk herniation, and intramedullary pathology (edema, hemorrhage, cord compression). CT myelography is used if MRI is contraindicated.

Physical Exam
  • Pin-prick/light-touch sensory testing across dermatomes
  • Motor testing of key muscle groups (C5–T1 upper extremity, L2–S1 lower extremity), graded 0–5
  • Deep tendon reflexes
  • Rectal exam for sacral sparing — voluntary anal contraction, deep anal pressure sensation
  • Vertebral column palpation/percussion
ASIA Impairment Scale (AIS)Definition
A — CompleteNo sensory or motor function preserved in sacral segments S4–S5
B — Sensory IncompleteSensory but not motor function preserved below the neurological level, including S4–S5
C — Motor IncompleteMotor function preserved below the level; more than half of key muscles below have a grade < 3 — usually cannot walk
D — Motor IncompleteMotor function preserved below the level; at least half of key muscles below have a grade ≥ 3 — usually can stand/walk
E — NormalSensory and motor function normal (reflexes may still be abnormal)
💡 Pearl — Sacral Sparing

Any preserved sacral function (voluntary anal contraction, deep anal pressure sensation) means the injury is not AIS A — this single exam finding can change the entire prognostic conversation with a patient and family.

Treatment
Management Overview

Surgical

  • Early decompression (within 24 hours) is associated with significantly better neurological outcomes — more than double the likelihood of a ≥ 2-point AIS improvement (RR 2.76)
  • Removal of compressive elements (bone fragments, disk material, hematoma)
  • Spinal stabilization/instrumentation when appropriate

Hemodynamic Management

  • Maintain MAP ≥ 85 mmHg for up to 7 days post-injury to optimize spinal cord perfusion, generally with ICU monitoring
  • Use caution with vasopressors (e.g., phenylephrine) — risk of pulmonary edema

Pharmacologic Therapy — Controversial

  • Methylprednisolone within the first 8 hours may reduce secondary injury via anti-inflammatory effects per some guidelines
  • Evidence is conflicting, higher doses carry more complications, and it is not universally recommended

Emerging Therapies

  • Cell-based/stem cell therapy: trials show feasibility and safety of intraspinal cell transplantation, but no therapy has yet fully restored function
  • Neuromodulation: epidural and functional electrical stimulation show promising improvements in motor, respiratory, and autonomic recovery
OMM Note

As with other acute CNS trauma, manipulative techniques directed at an unstable spine are contraindicated until the spine has been cleared and stabilized by the surgical team.

Monitoring & Long-Term Complications
System-by-System Complications
  • Cardiovascular: hemodynamic instability; autonomic dysreflexia (injuries above ~T6 — dangerous hypertensive episodes triggered by bladder/bowel distension); thromboembolic disease
  • Respiratory: respiratory failure, atelectasis, pneumonia; ventilator-dependent care for high cervical injuries
  • GI: ileus, constipation/impaction, gastric/duodenal ulcers
  • GU: UTIs (~62% cumulative incidence in year 1), neurogenic bladder requiring catheterization programs
  • Dermatologic: pressure ulcers (~41% cumulative incidence in year 1)
  • Musculoskeletal: osteoporosis (DEXA screening recommended), heterotopic ossification, fractures, overuse syndromes
  • Pain/spasticity: neuropathic + musculoskeletal pain (higher in motor-incomplete injuries); spasticity more common in motor-complete + cervical injuries, occasionally needing intrathecal drug delivery
⚠ Autonomic Dysreflexia

Seen with injuries above ~T6. An unchecked stimulus below the level of injury — most often a distended bladder or bowel — triggers a massive, unopposed sympathetic surge below the lesion (since descending inhibitory signals from the brain can't get past the injury), producing sudden severe hypertension with bradycardia, pounding headache, and flushing/sweating above the lesion. It's a medical emergency: sit the patient upright and search for and relieve the trigger (check the bladder/catheter and bowel first) while treating the blood pressure if it doesn't resolve.

Monitoring Pearl

Patients with motor-complete injuries (AIS A/B) have significantly higher rates of most secondary complications than motor-incomplete patients — systematic monitoring through the subacute and chronic phases is essential for early detection.

Prevention & Health Promotion
Adaptive Equipment & Functional Restoration
  • Adaptive equipment for ADLs, mobility, and independence
  • Phrenic nerve stimulation/diaphragmatic pacing for ventilator-dependent patients with injuries above C4 — freedom from mechanical ventilation, improved speech and mobility, lower healthcare costs
  • Functional electrical stimulation (FES) — muscle conditioning, locomotor training, prevention of disuse atrophy
  • Epidural electrical stimulation — promising results for locomotor and respiratory recovery
Bladder Management

Clean intermittent catheterization (CIC) is the preferred method — fewer complications/infections than continuous indwelling catheters. The Brindley-Finetech Vocare bladder system (sacral anterior root stimulator) is an option for bladder emptying in selected patients. Long-term urological surveillance protects renal function and prevents UTIs, hydronephrosis, and urolithiasis.

Skin & Bone

  • Skin integrity/pressure-relief programs
  • Osteoporosis screening with DEXA + fall prevention

Bowel & Sexual Health

  • Bowel continence programs
  • Sexual health and fertility counseling — pregnancy rates in cord-injured individuals have improved over the past decade

Respiratory & Thermal

  • Respiratory conditioning/preventive care
  • Thermal dysregulation awareness during exercise, particularly for injuries at T8 and above

Psychosocial

  • Psychosocial adaptation, vocational rehabilitation, and recreational skills training
Primary Prevention (of the Injury Itself)

Motor vehicle safety (seatbelts, airbags), fall prevention in the elderly, violence prevention, and sports safety measures remain the primary strategies for preventing traumatic SCI in the first place.

🧠 Practice Questions — Traumatic Spinal Cord Injury

💧 Hydrocephalus

LO 1–4 Communicating vs. Noncommunicating Evans Ratio > 30%
🎯 How Boards Would Word It
  • Elderly patient (> 60) with "wet, wacky, wobbly" — urinary incontinence, dementia, and a magnetic/shuffling gait — and notably no headache or papilledema (normal ICP) = normal pressure hydrocephalus
  • Infant with bulging fontanelle, macrocephaly, and the sunset sign (eyes deviated downward) = think obstructive/congenital hydrocephalus — open sutures buffer ICP, so neuro symptoms show up later than they would in an adult
  • MacEwen ("cracked pot") sign on skull percussion = a late finding from suture separation
  • A positive CSF tap test (gait improves after removing 30–50 mL of CSF) supports NPH and predicts shunt response
  • Key imaging distinction: ventriculomegaly without proportional sulcal enlargement = true hydrocephalus; ventriculomegaly with prominent sulci/cortical atrophy = hydrocephalus ex vacuo (not true hydrocephalus, normal ICP, no shunt needed)
  • Communicating = a CSF absorption/production problem (arachnoid villi, choroid plexus); noncommunicating = a mechanical obstruction, classically at the aqueduct of Sylvius
  • Post-shunt fever = shunt infection; post-shunt recurrence of ↑ICP signs = shunt obstruction — both are neurosurgical emergencies
Natural History
Epidemiology & Etiology
  • Congenital hydrocephalus accounts for ~60% of cases (~3 per 1,000 live births); acquired hydrocephalus accounts for ~40% and can affect any age
  • Normal pressure hydrocephalus, a common acquired form, primarily affects adults > 60
  • Male = female overall; communicating hydrocephalus is more common than noncommunicating
  • Etiologies span infection (meningitis), trauma (SAH/IVH), tumor, stroke/atrophy (ex vacuo), and congenital causes
  • Congenital causes: absence of arachnoid villi, Arnold-Chiari malformation, Dandy-Walker malformation (failure of the fourth ventricle to close, with cerebellar vermis hypoplasia and craniofacial/cardiac/spinal anomalies), intrauterine TORCH infections, colloid cyst, congenital aqueductal stenosis
Classification & Pathophysiology
CommunicatingNoncommunicatingEx Vacuo (not true hydrocephalus)
Mechanism↓ CSF absorption (arachnoid villi dysfunction, e.g., from meningitis or post-hemorrhagic scarring) or ↑ CSF production (choroid plexus papilloma/carcinoma)Mechanical obstruction of CSF flow — classically the aqueduct of Sylvius, or the foramina of Luschka/MagendieLoss of brain tissue (atrophy) passively enlarges the CSF spaces
Common causesMeningeal inflammation from infection or hemorrhageTumors (medulloblastoma, pinealoma, ependymoma, astrocytoma), colloid cyst, aqueductal stenosis, Dandy-Walker malformationAlzheimer disease, Huntington disease, frontotemporal dementia, AIDS, normal aging
Ventricles affectedAll ventricles dilateOnly ventricles upstream of the obstruction dilateVentricles and sulci enlarge together
ICPElevated (or normal in NPH)ElevatedNormal
⚠ Prognosis if Untreated

Most true hydrocephalus is progressive — left untreated, it can cause severe neurological damage, herniation, and death.

Clinical Presentation
Signs of Increased ICP (General)
  • Headache, vomiting (classically without nausea in children), blurred vision
  • Papilledema; abducens nerve palsy (a false localizing sign)
  • Unsteady gait, confusion, altered behavior or consciousness
  • Loss of energy/sleepiness, bladder incontinence
  • Cushing triad — a late, ominous finding
Infant manifestations of ↑ICP — bulging fontanelle, macrocephaly, prominent scalp veins, sunset eye sign, irritability, developmental delay, and poor feeding
An infant with macrocephaly and the setting sun sign — persistent downward eye deviation from pressure on the tectal plate/vertical gaze centers
Infant-Specific Features
  • Macrocephaly — head circumference > 2 SD above average for age and sex
  • Tense or bulging fontanelle
  • Setting sun sign — persistent downward eye deviation
  • Developmental delay, irritability, poor feeding
  • MacEwen ("cracked pot") sign — an unusually resonant sound on skull percussion from suture separation; a late finding
  • Lower extremity spasticity and hyperreflexia

Because an infant's fontanelles are still open, CSF accumulation can expand the head (macrocephaly) and partially offset the rise in ICP — so neurological symptoms often appear later than they would in an older child or adult with closed sutures.

Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus — The Classic Triad
  • Wet: urinary incontinence (initially urgency/frequency, which can be mistaken for a UTI)
  • Wacky: dementia — short attention span, loss of motivation, disorientation
  • Wobbly: gait apraxia — broad-based, short, shuffling ("magnetic") gait, frequent falls

NPH does not present with signs of elevated ICP (no headache, no papilledema) — ventricular dilation compensates for the slow CSF accumulation, keeping ICP normal or only mildly elevated.

🚩 Red Flags

Rapidly progressive macrocephaly, bulging fontanelle with lethargy or poor feeding, or any signs of herniation/Cushing triad warrant urgent neurosurgical evaluation.

Diagnostic Workup
History / Physical ExamLabs / Imaging
Infant < 18 months with an open anterior fontanelle Ultrasonography through the fontanelle
Older children (≥ 18 months) and adults MRI brain (preferred) or CT head — ventriculomegaly without (or out of proportion to) sulcal enlargement; Evans ratio (frontal horn width : biparietal diameter) > 30% supports the diagnosis
Determining subtype Communicating: all ventricles dilated. Noncommunicating: only ventricles upstream of the obstruction are dilated
Suspected NPH MRI (initial test): ventriculomegaly out of proportion to sulcal enlargement, periventricular white matter changes. CSF tap test: LP with opening pressure (typically normal/mildly elevated, 5–18 mmHg), then removal of 30–50 mL CSF with gait assessed before/after — improvement supports the diagnosis and predicts shunt response
Suspected meningitis or neoplastic seeding; need for opening pressure Lumbar puncture — only after intracranial mass lesions with mass effect are excluded on imaging, to avoid precipitating herniation
CT head, axial — dilated lateral ventricles (ventriculomegaly) consistent with hydrocephalus
MRI head, axial — markedly enlarged lateral ventricles, without proportional sulcal widening — the pattern expected in true hydrocephalus rather than ex vacuo
Noncommunicating hydrocephalus — cranial CT of a 13-year-old boy. A large, CSF-like hypodense lesion in the posterior fossa (likely an arachnoid cyst) compresses the cerebral aqueduct, obstructing CSF outflow. The third and lateral ventricles are dilated, with transependymal CSF egress visible on the lower images.
💡 Pearl — Hydrocephalus vs. Ex Vacuo

Ventriculomegaly without proportional sulcal enlargement points to true hydrocephalus. Ventriculomegaly with prominent, matching sulcal widening points to hydrocephalus ex vacuo — a passive consequence of brain atrophy, with normal ICP and no CSF flow abnormality, that does not require a shunt.

Treatment
Management Overview

Management is guided by neurosurgery. Because most hydrocephalus is progressive, treatment should begin promptly to avoid neurological damage.

Temporizing Measures

  • Serial lumbar punctures or lumbar drain — for communicating hydrocephalus
  • Ventricular tap — for preterm infants with intraventricular hemorrhage, via the open fontanelle
  • External ventricular drain — for noncommunicating hydrocephalus (e.g., after SAH)
  • Diuretics (furosemide, acetazolamide) to reduce CSF production, or intraventricular fibrinolytics after hemorrhagic hydrocephalus — benefit is limited

Definitive Surgical Treatment

  • Cerebral shunt (most commonly ventriculoperitoneal) — diverts excess CSF to another body cavity; components: inflow catheter, reservoir, valve, outflow catheter
  • Endoscopic third ventriculostomy — for obstruction at or distal to the aqueduct
  • Cerebral aqueductoplasty — opens a stenotic aqueduct
  • Excision of an obstructing lesion (e.g., posterior fossa tumor)
  • NPH: refer to neurosurgery for shunt placement; manage any secondary cause; supportive dementia care
Left: the NPH triad (dementia, urinary incontinence, magnetic gait) alongside reduced CSF absorption driving ventriculomegaly. Right: ventriculoperitoneal shunt anatomy — ventricular catheter, shunt valve, catheter tunneled under the skin, draining into the peritoneal cavity.
⚠ Shunt Complications — Neurosurgical Emergencies
  • Shunt infection: most commonly Staphylococcus epidermidis; presents with fever, headache, and signs of ↑ICP. Diagnose with CSF analysis/cultures. Treat with immediate neurosurgical consult for shunt removal plus antibiotics.
  • Shunt obstruction: presents with recurrent signs of ↑ICP. Diagnose with a shunt series and CT head. Treat with urgent shunt revision.
  • Overdrainage can cause intracranial hypotension or slit ventricle syndrome (chronic overdrainage → ventricular collapse and obstruction); underdrainage can lead to recurrent elevated ICP.
OMM Note

As with other conditions involving elevated or unpredictable intracranial pressure, cranial osteopathic techniques should be avoided in a patient with known or suspected hydrocephalus until cleared by neurosurgery.

🧠 Practice Questions — Hydrocephalus

👶 Shaken Baby Syndrome

LO 1–3 Nonaccidental Trauma SDH + Retinal Hemorrhage + Encephalopathy
🎯 How Boards Would Word It
  • An infant with no reported trauma history (or a history that doesn't match the injury severity) who has subdural hemorrhage + retinal hemorrhages + encephalopathy/seizures — this triad is the classic abusive head trauma pattern
  • A caregiver's story that changes over time or doesn't fit the injury ("he rolled off the couch," "she just wasn't acting right") is itself a red flag, not just a detail
  • Bilateral, multilayered retinal hemorrhages extending to the periphery are highly specific for abusive trauma rather than an accidental fall
  • Posterior rib fractures and metaphyseal "corner/bucket-handle" fractures found alongside head injury are classic markers of physical abuse (from a gripping/squeezing mechanism)
  • Subdural blood of different ages (acute mixed with chronic) on the same study suggests repeated episodes, not one accidental event
  • Any suspicion of abuse triggers a mandatory reporting obligation — this is not optional or dependent on parental consent
Natural History
Definition

Head trauma induced by rapid acceleration-deceleration events associated with child abuse — a form of nonaccidental trauma (abusive head trauma).

Mechanical & Vascular Pathophysiology
  • Violent shaking produces neck hyperflexion and hyperextension, jarring of the brain against the skull, and rib compression from the gripping hands
  • These forces cause shearing of cerebral vessels and axons, producing:

Intracranial

  • Diffuse cerebral edema
  • Diffuse axonal injury (DAI)
  • Epidural, subdural, subarachnoid, and intraparenchymal hemorrhage

Extracranial

  • Retinal hemorrhage (similar shearing/traction forces on retinal vessels)
  • Rib fractures (from the compressive grip)
Mechanism of injury — shearing forces on vessels and axons, jarring of the brain against the skull, neck hyperflexion/hyperextension, and rib compression, resulting in diffuse axonal damage, diffuse brain edema, retinal hemorrhage, subdural hematoma, and rib fractures
⚠ Prognosis if Unrecognized

Unrecognized or ongoing abuse can lead to severe, permanent neurological damage, developmental disability, or death. Repeated episodes are common in ongoing abuse and compound injury severity — which is exactly why early recognition and reporting are critical.

Clinical Presentation
Presenting Features
  • Focal and diffuse neurological complications
  • Subdural and subarachnoid hematoma (the most characteristic finding)
  • Lethargy, breathing difficulty, irritability, poor feeding, seizures
  • Altered consciousness and cognition
  • Emotional instability
  • Associated findings: retinal hemorrhage, rib fractures
🚩 Red Flags for Abuse
  • History inconsistent with the severity of injury, or a vague/changing account
  • No history of trauma at all despite significant clinical or imaging findings
  • Hemorrhages of different ages, suggesting repeated episodes
  • Associated fractures (especially posterior rib or metaphyseal) not explained by the stated mechanism
  • Any suspicion triggers a mandatory reporting obligation to child protective services
Diagnostic Testing
History / Physical ExamImaging
Caregiver history compared against injury severity; full physical exam including fundoscopic exam for retinal hemorrhage and exam for occult fractures MRI or CT head — evaluates for subdural/subarachnoid hemorrhage, diffuse axonal injury, and cerebral edema
Abusive head trauma — MRI head (axial) of a newborn presenting with seizures, fever, and vomiting. A/B: FLAIR shows crescentic supratentorial and infratentorial subdural hematomas, slightly hyperintense to parenchyma. C: SWI shows hypointense subarachnoid hemorrhage extending into right frontal sulci. D/E: DWI and ADC map show a right frontal cortical-subcortical hemorrhage (hyperintense on DWI, hypointense on ADC). F: One-month follow-up T2 shows bilateral crescentic subdural hygromas and encephalomalacia, isointense to CSF, with mass effect and a visible thin membrane.
Head trauma — CT head of a 7-week-old boy with reduced consciousness, showing a displaced calvarial fracture accompanied by an extra-axial hematoma and a cephalohematoma. A 7-week-old infant cannot self-mobilize into a mechanism that would produce this injury — while imaging alone cannot confirm nonaccidental trauma, the patient's age and the extent of injury should prompt consideration of abuse.
💡 Pearl — Why Multi-Sequence MRI Helps

Combining FLAIR, SWI, and DWI/ADC sequences helps identify blood products of different ages and subtle axonal injury that might be missed on CT alone — useful for recognizing the multi-age injury pattern that points toward repeated abuse rather than a single accidental event.
